summary: A report on Utah's experiments measuring host costs for sending network data. Utah had run compute-bound jobs on its PDP-10 and moved them to UCLA's batch machine. The note gives the background and examples of the jobs, and then the timing work.

eli5.summary: A school measured how much effort their computer spends just mailing data. They did it because they send many big jobs to a faster machine far away.

questions: host costs of network data transmission
subtitle: Utah measures how much host CPU time it costs to push data onto the ARPANET, and finds it surprisingly high.

tldr.problem: Utah sent big compute jobs from its TENEX PDP-10 to UCLA's batch service, and wanted to know what transmitting that data really cost the host.
tldr.mechanism: They timed the NETRJS program while it sent and received data, and computed real time, chargeable CPU time and microseconds per bit.
tldr.outcome: The cost came to 75 to 85 microseconds of CPU time per bit, about 33 to 37 times the predicted network transmission cost, so they argue for work on hosts and protocols.

today: RFC 392 has status Unknown and is not listed as updated or replaced. It is a 1972 measurement report on one host and one program.

sections.title: Why Utah Measured
sections.content:
Since October 1971, Utah had run very large compute bound jobs daily, such as algebraic simplification, partial differential equation solving and waveform processing. Treating them as batch work, in March they wrote a program to use the Remote Job Service (RJS) at UCLA-CCN, which runs on an IBM 360/91.

The protocol with RJS requires programs and data to be blocked, so Utah simulates records and blocks with special headers. This cost computation and core space, and page faulting led them to rewrite the sending and receiving parts so each fit in a little over half a page.
sections.eli5: Utah had giant jobs better suited to a bigger machine far away. Packing them up to send took more of their own computer's effort than they liked.

sections.title: Measurements and Results
sections.content:
On TENEX the network is accessed like a file, using byte-in (BIN) and byte-out (BOUT). The basic timing in fast mode is 120 us per byte. A slower step, once per message, averages 500 us for 36 bit bytes and may take up to a millisecond if bytes must be unpacked.

Timing showed 75 to 85 microseconds of chargeable CPU time per bit. The authors say they did not try to measure transmission rates, only how much it costs to take data from disk and send it to another host. The tables list clock time, CPU time, byte count, bits per second, microseconds per bit and load for many transfers between 13 and 19 September 1972.
sections.eli5: They used a stopwatch on every transfer. Each bit sent used a small slice of their computer's time, and the slices added up.

sections.title: Cost and Remedies
sections.content:
At a cost of $474.60 per CPU hour on TENEX, one million bits would cost $9.90 to $11.20 to transfer from the originating host, and potentially the same for the foreign host to receive. This is about 33 to 37 times higher than the predicted network transmission costs. In some cases, sending a program cost more than running it at the remote host.

Suggested remedies: treat the network as an interprocess communication device rather than a file device, build an intelligent network input/output device, and change the RJS-UCLA protocol, for example to allow 32 bit bytes instead of the required 8 bit bytes. The authors conclude that the work needed is on host machines and network protocols rather than the communication devices.
sections.eli5: The mailing was many times more expensive than people had guessed. They suggest smarter mail slots and simpler packing rules to fix it.
